questions.question: What does the Riemann integral formalise?
options: A relation between two sets
The reciprocal of a rational number
The successor of a natural number
Accumulation as the limit of finite sums
questions.explanation: The Riemann integral formalises accumulation as the common limit of increasingly fine finite weighted sums.
questions.source_support: The interpretation describes accumulation as the limit of finite sums.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: Set relations such as $A\subseteq B$ compare two sets by inclusion, whereas the Riemann integral is the limit $s=\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_i f(x_i^*)|J_i|$ of finite rectangle sums measuring accumulation.

A reciprocal is the multiplicative inverse $q\mapsto 1/q$ of a number, an algebraic operation on a single input; the Riemann integral instead aggregates $f$ over an interval via $s=\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_i f(x_i^*)|J_i|$.

The successor map $n\mapsto n+1$ is the inductive step on natural numbers, a discrete arithmetic function; the Riemann integral is the limiting sum $s=\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_i f(x_i^*)|J_i|$ over subintervals of $I$.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
